bd45bc61a3375664: SYDNEY, Oct 12 — Nearly one billion people worldwide are projected to be living with osteoarthritis by 2050, up from about 600 million in 2023, according to a roadmap released on Monday, reported Xinhua.

There remains no cure and no drug that can stop or slow the disease, prompting researchers to call for stronger health policies to address the growing global disability burden, according to a statement released on Monday by Australia’s Curtin University.

The global health policy roadmap published in The Lancet on World Arthritis Day by a Curtin University-led group of international researchers said osteoarthritis remained under-recognised in health policies globally, was often inadequately integrated into healthcare delivery for chronic diseases, and was inconsistently and often inappropriately treated and prevented.

The roadmap calls on governments to recognise osteoarthritis as a major chronic disease, improve access to evidence-based care, invest in prevention by addressing excess body weight and joint injuries, and integrate osteoarthritis care with broader chronic disease and rehabilitation services.

“Osteoarthritis faces an image problem — it’s perceived and dismissed in communities as an unavoidable part of aging with limited management options,” said the report’s lead author Professor Andrew Briggs from Curtin University.
Professor Lyn March, a co-senior author from Australia’s Kolling Institute, said the global disability burden attributed to osteoarthritis increased by 65 per cent between 1990 and 2023.
Rising obesity rates, population aging and increasing joint injuries are expected to drive further growth in cases in coming decades, the researchers warned. — Bernama-Xinhua
795bfdc990c04680: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Batik Air has cancelled its scheduled flight from Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, today as a precautionary measure amid the ongoing conflict.

790f535169c9ed5c: KUALA LUMPUR: The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is keeping a close watch on security developments in Riyadh ahead of continental club fixtures scheduled in the Saudi Arabian capital tonight.

The alert follows consecutive missile and drone strikes targeting King Khalid International Airport on Saturday and Sunday, which caused casualties, temporarily halted airport operations, and prompted regional flight cancellations and travel advisories.
The security scare coincides with matchday two of the revamped Asian Champions League Elite (ACLE) in the West Region.
Action in the capital is scheduled for tonight, with Cristiano Ronaldo's Al-Nassr hosting Uzbekistan's Neftchi at King Saud University Stadium at 9.15pm local time (2.15am Tuesday, Malaysian time).
When contacted by Timesport, AFC general-secretary Datuk Seri Windsor Paul John said the continental governing body is tracking ground assessments.
"We are monitoring the situation," Windsor said.

As of Monday afternoon, the Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF) has not issued any public statement or postponement directive regarding the airport strikes, with scheduled sporting events proceeding as planned under standard match-day protocols.
Neftchi's delegation, who arrived in Riyadh prior to the weekend airspace disruptions, completed their official pre-match technical briefings without schedule alterations.

However, the situation raises logistical questions for upcoming ACLE and Asian Champions League Two (ACL 2) fixtures, where visiting Asian clubs and AFC match officials rely on commercial flight corridors through Riyadh.
The developments also serve as a test for the kingdom's hosting roadmap.
Saudi Arabia will stage the Asian Cup from Jan 7-Feb 5 in several cities, including Riyadh, as well as the ACLE final on May 1.

In the past, the AFC has exercised contingency mechanisms, routinely shifting fixtures to neutral venues across the Gulf, such as the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman, whenever local airspace or ground conditions posed persistent safety risks.

On Sunday, Wisma Putra confirmed that no Malaysians were affected in the airport strikes, while advising travellers and residents in the kingdom to remain vigilant, verify flight schedules with airlines and adhere to local safety directives.
92dc834a4ed79c80: KUALA LUMPUR: Two cable theft incidents within hours of each other along the airport rail corridor have disrupted KLIA Ekspres and KLIA Transit services, resulting in longer journeys and schedule changes.
The thefts, which occurred between Sunday night and early today, involved about 260 metres of signalling cables along the railway line between Putrajaya and Salak Tinggi.

Express Rail Link Sdn Bhd (ERL), which operates both services, said the first incident was detected around 9pm yesterday near kilometre marker Km44, along the railway line between Putrajaya and Cyberjaya Station and Salak Tinggi Station.
The theft involved approximately 180 metres of signalling cables, comprising two 90-metre sections.
However, while technical teams were carrying out restoration works, a second act of vandalism was discovered at 5.22am today at KM42.
This time, another 80 metres of signalling cables, comprising two 40-metre sections, had been stolen.
The back-to-back incidents further complicated restoration efforts and disrupted normal train operations along the airport rail link.
"The incidents have extended restoration works and disrupted normal train operations," ERL said in a statement.

Following the disruptions, ERL initially introduced shuttle train services, requiring passengers travelling between KL Sentral and Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminals 1 and 2 to change trains at Putrajaya and Cyberjaya Station.
Under the temporary arrangement, trains operated at 15-minute intervals, with services departing KL Sentral for Putrajaya and Cyberjaya from 8.55am.
Services from KLIA Terminal 2 towards Putrajaya and Cyberjaya began at 9.05am.
ERL said train operations then resumed as a combined service at 11.20am, with trains running in both directions at 20-minute intervals.
However, technical teams were still working to fully restore the affected signalling system.
"Our technical teams are currently working to restore the system safely and as quickly as possible," it said.
ERL advised passengers using KLIA Ekspres and KLIA Transit services to factor in additional travelling time and plan their journeys accordingly.
"Passengers are advised to allow additional travel time and plan their journeys accordingly.
"We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience caused and appreciate the patience and understanding of all affected passengers," it said.

dd3023158675c8ae: A little-known doctoral student has emerged as one of the most visible faces of a protest movement in India that has mounted the most serious challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government in years.

Neha Bora, 29, is one of a number of prominent activists detained this weekend as the authorities cracked down on attempts by protesters led by the "Cockroach" youth movement to demonstrate against what they say is massive vote-rigging to help Modi's party.
But Bora, national president of the left-wing All India Students' Association, says she did not set out to become an activist.
She traces her path into politics to theatre and, later, the student-led protests against a citizenship law in 2019 and 2020.
On Saturday, after police blocked demonstrators from reaching New Delhi's designated protest site, Jantar Mantar, Bora urged them to regroup at Dilli Haat, a crafts market 10 km away.
"Dilli Haat becomes Jantar Mantar today," she wrote on X before setting off towards the site, chanting slogans as others followed.
Police detained her with several other activists. But even in detention, she called for the demonstration to continue.
"I am in detention. The movement is not," she said in a video posted online, urging supporters who were stopped by police to protest wherever they were. She was released later on Saturday.

The Cockroach Janta Party-led protests seek the ouster of India's election chief, claiming irregularities in handling voter data have led to the deletion of 130 million names — more than the population of Japan — from electoral rolls.

The Election Commission denies favouring any group, and Modi's Hindu nationalist party has accused opponents of trying to undermine the country's democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Other issues Bora has championed include school-examination scandals, unemployment and police actions.

Soft-spoken in conversation but forceful behind a microphone, she has built a following through speeches in Hindi and English, often invoking constitutional rights and linking student grievances to broader questions of inequality and government accountability.
Bora grew up in the Himalayan state of Uttarakhand and moved frequently as a child because her father served in the army.
She studied at Delhi University before beginning a doctorate at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of Arts and Aesthetics.
As an undergraduate, she told Reuters in an interview this month, she joined a theatre group, where she learned to inhabit the lives of people much different from herself.
"There might be a character that if you meet in your real life, you will disagree with, you will not like. But to do theatre is to understand where that person comes from."
A turning point was the citizenship law, which critics say discriminates against Muslims.

Bora said she watched students of her own generation lead classmates out of lecture halls and onto the streets, turning ideas she had encountered in books, films and documentaries into political action.
She gained wider attention during protests in July over alleged leaks of exam papers, when she joined other activists in demanding the resignation of the education minister.
Her speeches at Jantar Mantar, criticising the government and police response to demonstrators, circulated widely online.
Bora has since become a fixture at demonstrations in the capital.
During protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, she was repeatedly detained and returned to the streets after her release.
She said ideology alone does not drive the current mobilisation, describing hope as a more powerful force.
"Fear is infectious, of course. But hope is also infectious," she said. "People have courage now because they think that they can have courage."
Bora said the demonstrations reflect the accumulation of years of grievances.
"People remember," she said. "People carry that discontent, people carry that betrayal, people carry that disappointment."
* The writers are from Reuters

0470278e38fde5af: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Air quality worsened across the country this afternoon, with 23 of the nation's 68 monitoring stations recording unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings, according to the Department of Environment (DOE).

As of 4.50pm, 41 stations recorded moderate air quality and four were in the good range. No station recorded very unhealthy or hazardous levels. An Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 101 to 200 is classed as unhealthy.

Pasir Gudang in Johor recorded the highest reading at 174, followed by Kota Tinggi, also in Johor, at 170. Seremban in Negeri Sembilan was third at 167, followed by Pengerang in Johor at 166 and Nilai in Negeri Sembilan at 164.

Johor had seven stations in the unhealthy range. Besides Pasir Gudang, Kota Tinggi and Pengerang, the others were Larkin at 160, Batu Pahat at 156, Tangkak at 152 and Kluang at 151. Segamat, which was in the unhealthy range this morning, no longer appeared on the list.
Negeri Sembilan had three unhealthy stations, with Port Dickson at 154 in addition to Seremban and Nilai.

In Melaka, Bukit Rambai logged 161, Bandaraya Melaka 155 and Alor Gajah 153. Putrajaya recorded 156, up from 146 this morning and above the 150 mark that authorities there had cited as the closure threshold.
In Pahang, Balok Baru in Kuantan recorded 162 and Rompin 155. In Terengganu, Kemaman recorded 155 and Paka 153, while Johan Setia in Selangor stood at 152.

Unhealthy readings also appeared in East Malaysia, which was not among the areas listed this morning. In Sarawak, IPD Serian recorded 155, Sri Aman 153 and Samarahan 148, while in Sabah, Tawau logged 149.

Several readings have also risen since the morning. Pasir Gudang climbed from 168 to 174, Seremban from 164 to 167, and Bukit Rambai from 153 to 161. Alor Gajah in Melaka jumped from 101 to 153, Port Dickson from 137 to 154 and Johan Setia from 129 to 152. Kota Tinggi held at 170.
Earlier, Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek announced that schools in Johor, Melaka, Negeri Sembilan and Putrajaya will be closed tomorrow.

The closures also cover schools under the district education offices of Hulu Langat, Petaling Perdana, Kuala Langat and Sepang in Selangor, and Kuantan and Rompin in Pahang. Schools elsewhere will operate as usual.
Health and education authorities have advised parents, high-risk groups and students with respiratory symptoms to wear face masks and check real-time air quality updates through official channels.
fa39235661eb5380: BANGKOK, Oct 12 — Thai officials have found a nursing home where residents could be confined under metal bars fitted over their beds, in a scandal that is shining a light on how South-east Asia cares for its fast-growing older population.

Sothornchai Nursing Home in Kanchanaburi, western Thailand, came under scrutiny after a 63-year-old woman told a television programme she was held there for more than two years against her will, according to local and regional media reports.

Public Health Minister Pattana Promphat instructed the Department of Health Service Support (DHSS) to take immediate legal action if violations were found, the department said on its official Facebook page on October 6.

DHSS director-general Dr Phuwadet Surakot, who led the inspection, said officials found a room with iron bars and a lock on the outside, razor wire around the service area, and beds fitted with extra metal bars that could be closed over residents.
The home had 129 beds despite approval for only 50, and its service area had grown from the approved 1,600 square metres to 4,641 square metres, according to the DHSS.

Some residents did not fall within the categories the home was licensed to care for, including psychiatric patients taking medication and patients recovering from drug addiction, and their records held no medical certificates documenting their diagnoses, the department said.
Inspectors also reported no wastewater treatment system, cracked bathroom floors and insecticides stored alongside food ingredients, according to the DHSS.
The department said it would investigate the admission of psychiatric patients under the Health Establishment Act 2016 and consider suspending or revoking the home’s licence.
It revoked the licence on October 7, Nation Thailand reported.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Thai health officials inspect a nursing home in Kanchanaburi, western Thailand on October 6, 2026 where beds were found placed in rooms with metal bars and padlocked from the exterior. — Picture from Facebook/Department of Health Service Support
The owner defended the bed cages as a way to stop confused residents from falling, telling reporters on October 7 that they were for the residents’ protection, according to Thai media.
She later described the cages as an innovation in the care sector, seemingly unmoved by public anger over images of frail residents inside them.

The owner’s son told a Thai television programme on October 6 that he designed the cages himself as a safety measure after learning from incidents involving patients, Thai news outlet Khaosod English reported.
He said he was prepared to take responsibility for shortcomings in assessing patients and reviewing their medical records, and acknowledged that the cages’ design and appearance also mattered.
Thailand’s Department of Mental Health rejected the claim that the cages were standard psychiatric care, Nation Thailand reported.
Thailand has since ordered checks on about 1,200 registered care centres within two months.
The scandal strikes a nerve in South-east Asia because Thailand is the second-fastest ageing country in the region after Singapore, Hong Kong newspaper South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported.
Thirty per cent of Thais are expected to be aged 60 and above by 2035, according to the World Bank, although Thai authorities say that point could come sooner, the SCMP said.
“We have the personnel, but we don’t have the budget,” Thai Opposition MP and palliative care expert Ekkapop Sittiwantana was quoted as saying.
He said no Thai government has dared to fund long-term care through taxes or a dedicated fund for fear of losing votes, leaving families to carry the burden.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A nursing home in Kanchanaburi, western Thailand on October 6, 2026 where beds were found placed in rooms with metal bars or metal mesh and padlocked from outside. — Picture from Facebook/Department of Health Service Support

The pressure extends well beyond Thailand, with the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific estimating that 14 per cent of people in Asia and the Pacific were aged 60 or above in 2022, and projecting that the share will reach 26 per cent by 2050.
Singapore has already become a “super-aged” society, with 21.4 per cent of citizens aged 65 and above, according to the National Population and Talent Division’s Population in Brief 2026 report.
Malaysia is following the same path, with the Department of Statistics Malaysia estimating that 2.9 million people, or 8.4 per cent of the population, were aged 65 and above in 2026.

Women, Family and Community Development Minister Datuk Seri Nancy Shukri said on October 4 that Malaysia is expected to become an aged nation by 2036, when people aged 60 and above are projected to make up 15 per cent of the population, according to The Vibes.
Nancy said her ministry is drawing up a Strategic Framework and Care Action Plan 2026–2030 to set professional caregiving standards.
The Thai case shows what can happen when demand for care outgrows regulated capacity, a test that governments across the region are now facing.
5f6736ac2fc72d29: OCTOBER 12 — Imagine having access to almost everything that humanity has ever written, discovered or recorded, but not knowing what to do with it.
This would have sounded like a rather strange problem to our ancestors, who spent much of their lives trying to preserve knowledge and make it available to others.

Yet, in many ways, this is precisely the situation we find ourselves in today. We have more information at our fingertips than any generation before us, but having access to information does not necessarily mean that we know how to use it.
For much of human history, one of our greatest challenges was storing information.

Knowledge was passed from one generation to another through oral traditions, handwritten manuscripts and whatever materials were available at the time (including clay tablets used by the Sumerians and papyrus scrolls by the ancient Egyptians).
Even after papermaking developed in ancient China and gradually became more widespread, producing books remained laborious and expensive.
Access to written knowledge was largely confined to those who could afford it or had the privilege of entering institutions where such materials were kept.
The invention of the printing press by Johannes Gutenberg in the 15th century transformed this situation.
Books could be reproduced in greater quantities and distributed to a much wider audience.
Libraries, which had existed long before printing became widespread, gradually expanded their collections and their role in society.
Over time, knowledge that was once difficult to preserve and share became increasingly accessible.
Humanity had not completely solved the problem of storing information, but it had made remarkable progress.
However, this progress brought another challenge. As the amount of available information increased, finding what we needed became more difficult.
A library might contain thousands of books, but knowing which book held the answer to a particular question required another set of skills.
Then came computers, digitalisation and eventually the internet, followed by the World Wide Web, proposed by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
Information that previously required a visit to a library could now be accessed from almost anywhere.
Search engines further transformed this experience by allowing users to locate relevant information simply by entering a few keywords.
What once required hours of searching through books and journals could sometimes be accomplished within seconds.

Of course, the internet did not eliminate the problem of finding reliable information. In fact, the sheer volume of material available online created new difficulties, particularly when it came to distinguishing credible sources from questionable ones.
Nevertheless, the technological progress was undeniable. We had moved from worrying primarily about how to store information to developing increasingly sophisticated ways of finding it.

Today, with the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT and Gemini, we may be entering another phase in this long relationship with information.

Instead of searching through a list of websites and reading several sources to construct an answer, we can now ask a question in ordinary language and receive a response that appears to address our needs directly.
This introduces what I would call the third challenge: the problem of asking.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The ability to ask good questions becomes increasingly important. — Pexels pic
Unlike conventional search engines, large language models generate responses based on patterns and probabilities learned during their training.
They do not retrieve and reproduce knowledge in exactly the same way that a library catalogue or search engine does.
Their responses are influenced by how we phrase our questions, the context we provide and the instructions we include.
Two people seeking similar information may therefore receive quite different responses depending on how they approach the interaction.
This is where the ability to ask good questions becomes increasingly important.
A vague question may produce a general answer, while a more carefully considered question can lead to something considerably more useful.
Providing relevant context, explaining our intentions and identifying what we actually want to understand can improve the quality of the interaction.
Then there is also the question of what we do with the answers we receive.
Generative AI can produce convincing explanations even when the information is incomplete or incorrect.
Being able to ask a question therefore does not relieve us of the responsibility to examine the response, compare it with other sources and decide whether it makes sense.
Looking back, the history of information technology can be understood as a series of attempts to overcome different limitations.
We developed ways to preserve knowledge, then tools to locate it, and now systems that can respond to our questions in increasingly sophisticated ways.
Each development has expanded what ordinary people can do with information, while also requiring us to develop new skills.
Perhaps the most important skill for the next generation will not be the ability to remember more facts or even to find information more quickly.
It may be the ability to recognise what is worth knowing, formulate meaningful questions and exercise good judgement when answers are readily available.
So what do you want to ask today?

* Nahrizul Adib Kadri is a professor of biomedical engineering at the Faculty of Engineering, Universiti Malaya, who is currently pursuing an MA in Publishing Studies at the same university. He may be reached at nahrizuladib@um.edu.my

a9a81b0b54c0074b: It's 1988. Windows 2.0 is a DOS shell that runs on a dual-floppy 8086 PC. VGA is the aspirational video standard. A three-man startup in East London has decided to create low-cost LANs. There's not much of that and not much by way of standards, which is why a young programmer is rather excited by an emerging contender called TCP/IP. He's particularly keen because he's just finished implementing IBM's PC networking API, NetBIOS, which hurt almost as much as integrating any sort of networking with DOS. Research means library books, magazine articles, and asking questions on Usenet over kilobit dial-up. Getting the wrong idea is easy. Trying to build the TCP/IP stack on the ISO/OSI seven-layer model produces more pain, but sanity prevails, and after a bit, there's a working network. Nearly 40 years later, the once-young programmer is now a curmudgeonly Reg columnist. Floppies have become terabyte thumb drives. Kilobit modems are gigabit fiber and Wi-Fi. Graphics have come on a bit too. And he hasn't touched Windows or an Intel CPU in years. It is a transformed world. Except for one thing – everything talks to everything over TCP/IP. It's time to celebrate the digital oxygen of the global data ecosystem. TCP/IP is still newsworthy. Any apparent attempt to replace part of it is worth reporting, in this case a congestion-easing protocol called Homa superseding TCP. Only it's not a replacement, just an alternative designed to run alongside. That this is possible is due to one of the genius decisions made as TCP/IP evolved – splitting what was one protocol into two: TCP and IP. IP, the Internet Protocol, just sends packets between two addresses, best effort, no guarantees when, in what order, or even if they'll get through. The Transmission Control Protocol uses IP but delivers a reliable, ordered stream of bytes, arranging retransmission of missing data. Thus, if you don't like how TCP does things, you can add your own IP-speaking protocol to run alongside. This approach also saw TCP/IP vanquish rival protocols from very large industry incumbents, such as IBM's Systems Network Architecture (SNA) and ATM – Asynchronous Transfer Mode – from the telecoms side. Packet-switched IP can't possibly succeed, they said, with its non-deterministic transmissions of unknown latency. Nothing reliable could be built on that. TCP/IP, being open, flexible, and built by consensus by individual, inspired engineers, just got on with being useful. That had been proved on January 1, 1983, when ARPANET – the proto internet – dropped the proto when it switched over wholesale from its own NCP to TCP/IP. Known as flag days, such events weren't uncommon as previously isolated early networks had to adapt or die to the new interconnected world. TCP/IP was explicitly designed to inter-network, from the seminal paper [PDF] in 1974 by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn. From that 13-page paper to adoption across ARPANET took nine years. Five years later, a greenhorn coder could build the stack for completely novel hardware in three months. It took longer to work out how to build an installable driver for IBM's PS/2 Micro Channel Architecture. The future wasn't hard to see. Once it had beaten the opposition, the extremely practical, extremely open soul of TCP/IP repeatedly saved it from its biggest enemy. Itself. It turned out that once we had a technology that could freely connect any number of devices to each other, end to end, we wanted to do that very much. The internet, freed of central control and gatekeepers, grew exponentially, especially after another protocol, HTTP, shyly perched on top of TCP. Naysayers predicted letting ordinary people use this would clog the internet, to the point that the introduction of image tags was seen as portending the End Times. Congestion collapse could close it all down. Fortunately, shortly before Tim Berners-Lee began work on the Web, a 1988 paper by Van Jacobson and Mike Karels, Congestion Avoidance and Control [PDF], came up with a set of strategies and tweaks to TCP that has kept the problem at bay ever since. A global network with no central control that can fix show-stopping, scale-related problems on the fly is a true wonder. Similarly, IPv4's 32-bit address field with 4.3 billion addresses seemed an over-provision, until suddenly it was nowhere near enough. A new version of IP, IPv6, was introduced in 1995 with addresses as plentiful as grains of sand in the Sahara. The trouble was that if you've got billions of devices, you can't do a flag day. IPv6 proved great for infrastructure, but not the edge. Fortunately, a router kludge called Network Address Translation (NAT) appeared, again at roughly the same time. It broke the end-to-end principle only a little bit, but let the old version of IP, IPv4, run untouched. Let's be frank. It's fugly. But it let many devices share a single public IP address, which is why everything that comes out of the box for normies still rocks IPv4 like it's 1981. Just don't ask what happened to IPv5. There are thousands of ways TCP/IP has evolved, many tiny and a few deeply silly, like RFC 1149 (IP over Avian Carriers), material relating to which is, at the time of writing, up for auction at Christie's. At heart, it is one of mankind's most brilliant technical achievements, the underpinning of everything the connected world can do, built from intelligence, vision, openness, iteration, freedom of thought, freedom of action, a rough consensus and running code. It deserves its own universal day of celebration. Let's make it January 1. Let's call it Flag Day. ®
e3ac5ffe7bd042d2: OCTOBER 12 — The National Environment Agency (NEA) will launch a two-year pilot ferry service for the scattering of cremated remains at sea in the second half of 2027, it said today.
The pilot is being introduced in response to growing demand for ash scattering as the number of cremations in Singapore rises.
“As Singapore’s population ages, demand for after-death services is expected to grow,” the agency stated.
The ferry service will operate weekly from Pasir Panjang Ferry Terminal, under the management of an operator appointed by NEA.
Multiple groups will be allowed to board each vessel for cost-effectiveness. A fee of $50 per application applies, NEA said.
The agency will monitor uptake of the service and gather feedback to assess the service’s long-term viability.
More details on the pilot ferry service, including the ash scattering site, booking arrangements and procedures, will be released ahead of its launch in 2027.
The agency also shared that annual deaths are expected to increase from 26,500 in 2025 to about 40,000 by 2040.
Currently, around 82 per cent of those who pass away in Singapore are cremated, with take-up of inland ash scattering growing since the option was introduced in 2021.
The proportion of cremations where ashes were scattered at inland ash scattering facilities rose to about 12 per cent in 2025, up from about seven per cent in 2022.

According to findings from the Study on Wake Spaces conducted by the Institute of Policy Studies at the National University of Singapore, around 42 per cent of respondents indicated a preference for ash scattering.
As for the type of ash scattering, 27 per cent shared their preference for ash scattering at sea, while 15 per cent preferred utilising inland facilities.
At present, the agency has been expanding capacity across government-managed facilities, such as the opening of The Garden of Serenity at Mandai North Crematorium in August 2025.
The Garden of Serenity is Singapore’s second inland ash scattering facility.

NEA deputy chief executive officer and director-general of public health Chew Ming Fai said that as needs and preferences evolve, the agency is committed to providing “more options for people making after-death arrangements for their loved ones”.
“This pilot will make the scattering of ashes at sea more accessible, while allowing us to better understand demand and shape the service to meet their needs.” — AsiaOne

1a3b39f6f7422e35: The quirky vase, the owl candlestick, my mother’s ring – these items hold part of me and carry with them an existential problem A friend of mine recently discussed his will with me. He talked about the importance of looking after his daughter financially when he’s gone. As a child-free woman, I confidently told him my money will go to organisations that have meant something to me: Macmillan Cancer Support and animal charities. It bemuses me how people think the absence of children is a problem when it comes to inheritance money; it’s always been obvious to me that I’d give my money to causes that touch my heart. But then my friend served something of a curveball. He asked me who will have my deceased mother’s ring? It made me think: where do the precious artefacts from our lives go when we are no longer here? Whenever I’m away from home I look forward to being reunited with these things: the quirky vase that sits in the window of my study, and the owl candlestick, a birthday gift from my potter friend. These items carry parts of me – what will become of them? If you have children, the answer to this question is not presented to you as a puzzle; like a constellation of stars, the answer is perfectly aligned. If you don’t have children, the question can lead to existential angst. Kiran Sidhu is a freelance journalist and writer. She is the author of I Can Hear the Cuckoo. She also wrote the Bafta award-winning documentary Heart Valley. Continue reading...
56ce85f478edcf8f: HONG KONG: Action star Donnie Yen's 69-year-old mother-in-law, Jennifer Wang, has caught the internet's attention with her youthful appearance, prompting netizens to say she looks more like her granddaughter's mother than her grandmother.
Jennifer, the mother of Yen's wife, former beauty queen Cissy Wang, 45, recently celebrated her birthday.
Her granddaughter, Jasmine Yen, 21, shared a video of the celebration on Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu.
In the video, Jennifer appeared in a floral spaghetti-strap dress, showing off her slim figure as she posed alongside Jasmine.
Her youthful appearance and elegant presence quickly became the focus of online discussion.
Some netizens said the pair looked more like mother and daughter than grandmother and granddaughter, despite their 48-year age gap.

c0028eb4231bbf42: LABUAN, Oct 12 — The natural sand spit on Kuraman Island has set two national records in the Malaysia Book of Records (MBR), with its total length measuring 808.4 metres and its exposed section measuring 790.4 metres.

The two records are ‘Longest Natural Sand Spit in Malaysia’ (Beting Pasir Semula Jadi Terpanjang di Malaysia) and ‘Longest Exposed Sand Spit in Malaysia’ (Beting Pasir Terdedah Terpanjang di Malaysia).
The certificate recognising the achievements was presented to Federal Territories Department director-general Datuk Muhammad Azmi Mohd Zain following the official declaration.

Muhammad Azmi said the recognition marked a significant milestone in efforts to promote Labuan’s geological heritage and tourism potential, while raising the profile of Kuraman Island and Labuan Geopark nationally.

Located west of Labuan near Rusukan Besar and Rusukan Kecil islands, Kuraman Island covers about 1.47 square kilometres (363 acres) and is the largest island in the Labuan Marine Park, which was gazetted in 1994.
The island’s main attraction is its natural sand spit, a distinctive geological formation extending into the sea.
Estimated to be about 35 million years old, it was formed through sediment deposition and the combined effects of longshore currents, waves and wind.

“The two MBR records were awarded based on measurements of the natural formation’s total length and exposed section. The recognition is expected to strengthen the island’s appeal as a geotourism destination, complementing its marine ecosystem, coastal scenery and distinctive geological landscape.

“It could also create opportunities for nature-based tourism and community-driven economic activities, including boat transport, recreational services, tour guiding, hospitality and small businesses,” he said to Bernama at the site today.
However, he said tourism development must be carried out responsibly to safeguard the island’s geological heritage and marine ecosystem.

“Kuraman Island is one of the key geosites under Labuan Geopark, offering visitors an opportunity to appreciate the relationship between geological history, marine biodiversity and coastal processes,” he said.

Muhammad Azmi said the recognition would support efforts to position Labuan as a tourism destination with a distinctive identity while ensuring the island’s natural heritage remains protected for future generations. — Daily Express
58896fc479fb14e2: KUALA LUMPUR: Banks have given interim assurances that they will not pressure the families of 54 Malaysians who remain missing following flash floods in Nepal, Malaysia Solidarity Families in Hope (Masfih) said.

Its coordinator and spokesperson, Dr R. Manivannan, said the assurance followed a two-and-a-half-hour meeting at Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) involving financial institutions, insurance companies and the next of kin of the missing Malaysians.
"Banks have assured the families that they will not pursue loan repayments or other payments until an agreement is reached," he said.
Manivannan said Masfih welcomed the commitment but was still awaiting a written framework from BNM outlining measures to protect the families from further financial hardship.
"We have stopped the bleeding but not treated the injuries," he said, stressing that the families needed a clear, coordinated solution to address their loved ones' outstanding financial commitments.
A catastrophic flood struck the Himalayas on Aug 26 after a mountain and glacier collapsed near Nepal's border with China.
More than 1,400 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing after tsunami-like waves swept through mountainous areas in the north, destroying homes, roads, bridges and settlements.

Manivannan said Masfih had submitted a 35-page proposal to BNM outlining financial relief measures, including a mechanism to address outstanding loans, credit commitments and liabilities while the missing individuals' status remained unresolved.

The meeting also sought to establish a coordinated approach involving BNM, financial institutions and relevant government agencies so families would not have to deal with banks and insurers individually.
Manivannan said the interim assurance was a positive first step but should not be treated as a substitute for a formal policy covering the families' financial concerns.
"We need a written and comprehensive framework so that the families know exactly what protection is available to them and how they can access it," he said.
He said Masfih wanted an urgent meeting with the Prime Minister to facilitate a coordinated government response and secure clear assurances on the way forward.
"The families need to know what can be done, how it can be done and what the next steps are," he said.
69514a6c4d38cb46: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Schools across Johor, Melaka, Negeri Sembilan, and Putrajaya, as well as several districts in Selangor and Pahang, will be closed tomorrow following a sharp deterioration in air quality, Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek announced today.

In a statement posted on her official Facebook page, Fadhlina confirmed that all primary and secondary schools in the three states and the federal administrative centre will suspend physical classes tomorrow.

The mandatory closures also extend to schools under four District Education Offices (PPD) in Selangor: Hulu Langat, Petaling Perdana, Kuala Langat, and Sepang. In Pahang, schools under PPD Kuantan and PPD Rompin will likewise remain closed.
Schools in all other unaffected states and districts will operate as normal, the minister said.

The nationwide shutdown follows a sudden rebound in transboundary smoke pollution, with Department of Environment (DOE) data recording 22 out of 68 national monitoring stations in the unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) bracket (101 to 200) earlier today.

Johor was the hardest hit nationwide, logging eight unhealthy stations led by the country's peak reading of 170 in Kota Tinggi. In Negeri Sembilan, Seremban registered 164 and Nilai recorded 163. In Pahang, Balok Baru in Kuantan posted 162 and Rompin stood at 157, while Bukit Rambai in Melaka recorded 153. Putrajaya logged 146, nearing the 150 closure threshold.
Several affected districts had only resumed physical classroom sessions this morning after experiencing moderate air quality over the weekend.

Health and education authorities have urged parents, educators, and high-risk students with chronic respiratory conditions to wear protective face masks outdoors and closely track hourly API updates via official channels.
d4674044ef80df92: JOHOR BARU: School closures due to the haze have left some parents in Johor scrambling to manage their children's online lessons, with limited devices and supervision posing major challenges.
Nor Azura Md Amin, 40, said her three children, aged six, eight and 10, had to attend online classes simultaneously, despite having only two devices at home.
"It was complete chaos when classes started simultaneously. I only have two devices at home, but three children need to access their classes.
"Not only do we lack devices, but when there are topics that they do not understand, all three would ask me questions at the same time," she said when contacted.
Azura, who works in the private sector, said the situation had disrupted her daily routine and she might have to take leave if the haze persisted.
"Luckily, today is my day off. Last week, no one was able to guide and monitor the children during online classes because both my husband and I were working.
"The challenge is even greater for residents in rural areas due to slow internet connectivity, making it difficult for children to follow their lessons smoothly," she said.
Another parent, Siti Hajar A Gaffar, 43, said some parents had not been allowed to work from home during the home-based teaching and learning (PdPR) period.
She said this made it difficult for parents to supervise their children, particularly primary school pupils who were left without adult supervision at home.
"This affects the children's concentration during online lessons because no one is available to monitor them throughout their classes.
"Device limitations are also a major problem, as some older personal devices, such as outdated iOS devices, do not support essential applications such as Google Meet," she said.
All schools in Johor were closed last Thursday and Friday amid worsening air quality and public health concerns.
The state government has extended the closure for another five days, from today until Friday.

The closure affects 1,198 schools and 617,258 students, as well as 575 Johor State Religious Schools, three Johor State Religious High Schools and 239 registered Private Islamic Educational Institutions in the state.
